Your bike means more than you might realize. It's fitness, it's transportation, it's recreation, and it can be a vital part of your physical and mental well-being. Protect it. Bicycle riding peaks in the warmer months of the year. So does bicycle theft. Here in the northern hemisphere, that time is almost upon us. Don't be a victim.

* Don't assume you're safe. Cyclists are much more likely to experience theft. Some bike thieves even have people who notify them when there is a potential target bike parked nearby. Some bike thieves even stalk potential victims with high-end bikes to learn their habits and where to strike. A cheap or beat up looking bike is not immune to being stolen either. Some thieves are desperate enough to take anything or are just looking for something to ride across town where they may simply ditch it. * If you use Strava, don't start and stop it at your house. Some thieves use Strava to locate and stalk potential targets. Consider setting your Strava profile to private if you're really paranoid about the possibility that thieves in your area might be doing this. * If you don't want to carry a lock, then don't take your bike where you'll need one. Not carrying a lock is totally fine if you're going to be riding out in the countryside somewhere, but it's probably not okay to go without a lock while you're making stops in the city. * If you have no lock, keep in mind that your bike won't be stolen if it's always with you. If you have to stop somewhere, don't leave your bike alone. Confidently wheel it inside with you. You'd be surprised how often you can do this. If someone tries to stop you, be polite and try to negotiate. Ask if you can leave it propped up just inside the entrance where it won't be stolen. Chances are good that they will allow it, and you might even be able to enlist an employee to watch it for you! People can be very sympathetic if you give them a chance. Leaving it at customer service desks is usually a viable option too. If you can't take it inside, leave. Go somewhere else. If that's not an option, then put the bike against a large window where you can see it clearly at all times, and don't walk farther away from it than about 10-15 feet. * A folded bike can be wheeled or carried almost everywhere that a normal bike wouldn't be allowed. * Don't use cable locks. They are worthless. Thieves will cut through them with a simple set of wire cutters in the time it takes to snap your finger. Many chains are just as dumb to use because they simply aren't thick enough to withstand simple brute forcing with bolt cutters. Even a heavy chain can often be defeated by something as simple as smashing the lock against the pavement. * A U-lock (alternately known as a D-lock) is best, but not foolproof. Against an average thief, a good quality U-lock will usually deter them, especially if there are other bikes nearby which will be easier for them to steal. Against a good thief who is prepared, it will only buy you a minute or two of time before they can defeat it and steal your bike. * No lock is completely secure, but some are better than others. A cheap U-lock is almost worthless. Thieves can often spot the cheap ones as they will have seen them frequently and will likely know how to defeat them with ease. Sometimes thieves will even buy U-locks so they can take them home and figure out how to beat them. Locks also often have attack methods posted online. Try searching online for attack methods against the lock(s) you currently own lock if you want to be horrified. * Don't count on having your bike replaced by lock manufacturers if it gets stolen. The manufacturers that offer these replacement guarantees almost ***never*** pay out to theft victims. You might as well consider these guarantees to be a lie. They effectively are. * When locking your bike, locking it somewhere you can keep an eye on it is usually better than locking it up to a dedicated bike rack. * Don't simply lock the bike to itself and walk away for an instant thinking this will be enough. Someone can simply carry your bike away. * Avoid locking your bike to insecure objects like benches, sign posts, trees, anything flimsy, or anything not bolted to the ground. Thieves can easily cut through or break wooden benches, trees, or cheap metal and steal your bike along with the lock. They can also simply lift your bike along with the lock over the sign post you were dumb enough to use. Sometimes this may require them to unscrew the sign, but they'll do it. * Watch out for "sucker poles". These are bike racks that might look secure, but they have been sabotaged to make stealing your bike easy for a thief. Sometimes they will cut through a bike rack and cover the cut with tape or stickers, or they will un-anchor one or more of the legs so they can simply lift it up and slide off your bike. * Practice good locking technique. Locking around the rear wheel through the rear triangle of the bike frame is best. Watch proper locking method videos on youtube. * At home, your bike is still safer in the house where you can see it. In the garage or the shed isn't as safe as you might think. Bike thieves target those locations too.
